item.title: InletScope: Multiscale pressure-based inlet unstart monitoring under changing sensor configurations
item.description: arXiv:2611.31246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Supersonic inlets capture and compress air for aeroengines, and unstart can disrupt the air supply and compromise propulsion-system stability. Pressure-based monitoring must accommodate flow responses that vary with operating condition and measurement location. InletScope combines shared multiscale pressure encoding, learned scale fusion and sensor-probability averaging, allowing measurement sets to change without retraining. Separate models evaluate unstart detection and new-onset prediction within a 0.5-s future interval. Seven Mach-2.9 runs, each with one annotated event, cover downstream throttling, throat regulation and splitter adjustment; three are held out with fixed weights and source-derived settings. Across three training seeds, full-sensor detection achieves run-wise mean window $F_1$ scores of 0.834--0.964. Eight-sensor aggregation reduces detection-score variation across sensor subsets in both splitter runs while retaining mean scores close to those of the full sets. Regional detection favors cowl and high-speed-channel measurements during splitter adjustment and compression-side measurements during downstream throttling, consistent with their respective pressure responses. Complete-record evaluation shows that configurations with comparable window scores can produce different alarm timing and persistence. These findings connect sensor count and regional coverage to pressure discrimination and sequential alarm behavior, providing experimental guidance for configuring inlet monitoring systems.
item.dc:creator: Jiaming Liu, Fenlou Zhai, Ao Xue, Liangliang Tang, Cheng Ding, Daoqiang Zhang

item.title: Bayesian approach to the Student's t-test based on the B-FBST
item.description: arXiv:2611.31400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article proposes an exact Bayesian formulation of the B-FBST Student's t-test applied to the one-sample Student's t-test. The method relies on constructing an exact posterior distribution of the standardized parameter, then calculating the e-value to measure the evidence against the null hypothesis. To improve the stability of the procedure, posterior densities obtained from bootstrap samples are aggregated using random weights. A Monte Carlo simulation study was then conducted to compare the B-FBST Student's t-test with the classical Student's t-test and the bootstrap Student's t-test. The results, obtained from 100 Monte Carlo replications and 200 bootstrap replications, show that the B-FBST Student's t-test exhibits favorable overall performance, with an average of 71.0% correct decisions, compared to 65.5% for the classical test and 70.7% for the bootstrap test. The proposed method thus appears to be a robust alternative, particularly in several situations where the classical assumptions of the Student's t-test are compromised.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Hamimes

item.title: Probabilistic index models for hierarchical survival outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2611.31624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In clinical trials, prioritized composite outcomes allow treatment comparisons to reflect the clinical importance of fatal and nonfatal events. Probabilistic index models relate these comparisons to covariates, but censoring can leave a comparison unresolved. We develop three weighted estimating equations at a prespecified restriction time, with logit, probit, and identity links. Complete history weighting requires both restricted histories to be observed. Resolved comparison weighting also retains comparisons determined before both histories are complete. Conditional tie weighting further uses an observed lower-priority event when higher-priority ties remain uncertain, weighting its regression residual by their conditional probability under a joint model of observed event histories. The construction accommodates a fixed number of nonfatal components and parametric or semiparametric joint models. Under their respective nuisance-model assumptions, the three equations target the same full data regression parameter. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality and derive sandwich estimators accounting for overlapping pairs and nuisance estimation. Across 27 simulation configurations, conditional tie weighting had smaller empirical variance than the other two methods, with reductions ranging from 5.1 to 59.0 percent relative to resolved comparison weighting. An HF-ACTION analysis of death and first hospitalization illustrates the additional observed information used by conditional tie weighting. Conditional tie weighting yielded smaller estimated variances, and the treatment effect intervals from all three methods included zero.
item.dc:creator: Xi Fang, Zhiqiang Cao, Lu Mao, Fan Li

item.title: Correcting for Differential Nonresponse Using Past Election Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.31662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In an election survey, the probability of responding can depend on the vote being measured. When supporters of one candidate are less likely to respond, they are underrepresented in the sample and the estimated vote share is biased. Weighting and multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) adjust for observed covariates but do not eliminate this bias when response rates differ by vote within demographic groups. We ask whether this differential nonresponse can be corrected using the previous election, whose outcome is known. We estimate a two-parameter correction on the log-odds scale against one election's results, apply it unchanged to the next, and compare the corrected estimates with its results. The application is the Cooperative Election Study for the 2020 and 2024 U.S. presidential elections, with the 436 congressional districts as units. Among validated voters in 2020, Republicans appear in the sample at about 0.6 times the odds of Democrats, and in both elections district-level MRP understates the Republican two-party share by 16 to 18 percentage points on average. A correction estimated on 2020 and applied to 2024 gives 95% posterior predictive bands containing the actual result in 98.2% of districts, compared with 91.5% for a correction on the share scale. About two-thirds of the curvature in the 2024 error was already present in 2020, and the transferred correction removes about 69% of it; the remaining third, a level shift of 1.7 points, and a few districts (several with very large 2020-to-2024 swings) are specific to 2024. We also fit a model for variation in differential nonresponse across districts (Little and Gelman, 1998) and find that the design weights account for about 62% of the selection on the log-odds scale. Two variants that apply the correction within poststratification cells, specified in advance, did not improve on the simpler correction.
item.dc:creator: David Metrick, Harper Wang

item.title: Differential Item Functioning: Methodological Advances in Detection, Identification, and Interpretation
item.description: arXiv:2611.31696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differential item functioning (DIF) occurs when an item's response distribution differs across groups for respondents at the same level of the construct. Separating DIF from group differences in the construct itself requires identifying assumptions. Conventional analyses compare observed groups on a common scale established through items assumed to be invariant. We distinguish four settings according to whether the groups are observed or latent and whether the common scale is fixed by prespecified restrictions or estimated from the data. For observed groups, we review observed-score and item response theory procedures, multiple-covariate and intersectional models, and recursive partitioning. When anchors are unknown, we compare empirical anchor selection, partial and approximate invariance, robust scaling, regularisation and sparsity-based identification by the assumptions each makes about the pattern of DIF. For latent groups, we discuss mixture models and the joint estimation of class membership and DIF. Further topics include ordinal and multidimensional models, inference after data-dependent selection, effect sizes, consequences for composite scores, and the sources of DIF. We conclude with open problems, including anchor-free identification when DIF is widespread and inference when latent classes and invariant items are selected jointly.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Wallin, Qi Huang

item.title: Aalen-Johansen as an augmented IPCW estimator
item.description: arXiv:2611.32026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that, in every sample, the widely used Aalen-Johansen estimator of a state occupation probability is an inverse probability of censoring weighted estimator augmented by a working Markov prediction from each subject's current state. This identity explains the robustness of the Aalen-Johansen against departures from the Markov assumption. It also reveals that its influence function differs from the semiparametric efficient one by two orthogonal components: the information in earlier history beyond the current state, and the error of the Markov prediction. Based on this decomposition, we propose a practical, model-free least-squares augmentation of the Aalen-Johansen that regresses the outcome on a history score, narrowing the gap under non-Markov processes without increasing the asymptotic variance. Its advantages are validated both theoretically and in simulations.
item.dc:creator: Lu Mao

item.title: Nonparametric Change-Point Detection for Modern Data: Representations and Statistical Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2611.32158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonparametric change-point methods for high-dimensional and non-Euclidean data, including networks and covariance matrices, compare observations through a representation: coordinates, kernels, distances, similarity graphs, ranks, or learned scores. These representations affect which changes a method can detect and what the reported evidence means. We review retrospective methods by relating their representations to the population discrepancies targeted by their scores, the search over change times, the calibration of that search, and the resulting statistical guarantee. We distinguish population identification, detection power, scan-level error control, and localization, and examine these guarantees for multiple changes, dependent sequences, objects estimated from replicates, and online monitoring. Simulation experiments illustrate these distinctions: two scores on the same nearest-neighbor graph have similar power but give different location estimates. These comparisons guide the choice of a representation that preserves the change of scientific interest and a procedure whose guarantee supports the intended inference.
item.dc:creator: Hoseung Song

item.title: Asymptotically Efficient Conformal Inference for Individual Treatment Effects under Multivalued Treatments
item.description: arXiv:2611.32182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most existing conformal inference methods for individual treatment effects are limited to settings with binary treatments. For multiple treatments, propensity score-derived weights often suffer from statistical instability, while contiguous prediction intervals may span low-density regions between modes of potential outcome distributions, leading to inefficient prediction sets. We propose adaptive prediction sets for counterfactual outcomes under multivalued treatments by combining KuLSIF-based density ratio estimation with highest predictive density (HPD) conformal scores derived from conditional density estimates. Both estimators share a reproducing kernel Hilbert space least-squares formulation, which simplifies theoretical derivation and analysis. The resulting prediction sets are robust to heteroscedasticity and multimodal outcome distributions and effectively eliminate low-density regions between distribution modes. Under unconfoundedness assumption and regularity conditions, we prove that the proposed method converges to optimal HPD sets under covariate shift and establish its asymptotic conditional validity and statistical efficiency. Simulation studies and ACIC benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves empirical coverage probabilities close to the nominal level, while yielding shorter average interval lengths than conventional quantile-based conformal methods for multimodal outcome data.
item.dc:creator: Lequn Ge, Gaorong Li, Hui Zhao

item.title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs
item.description: arXiv:2611.32415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $\beta\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\ge\beta$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.
item.dc:creator: Ruiqi Zhao

item.title: Partial Identification under Imperfect Compliance via Cross-World Correlation Restriction
item.description: arXiv:2611.32615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article develops a unified partial identification approach for the average treatment effect (ATE) and the local average treatment effect (LATE) in randomized experiments with imperfect compliance, incorporating the cross-world correlation between potential treatment statuses. Even under random assignment and exclusion restriction, the correlation is unidentified. However, given the two identified marginals, it uniquely determines the relative proportions of the four principal strata, with monotonicity corresponding to a special case. We derive explicit sharp bounds for both the ATE and LATE at a fixed correlation and extend the results to prespecified correlation ranges, providing a sensitivity analysis that incorporates substantive information about compliance behavior. For the ATE, the lower bound decreases and the upper bound increases with the correlation. Although imposing monotonicity does not tighten the conventional Balke--Pearl bounds, we show that restricting the correlation can yield tighter bounds, even when defiers remain possible. For the LATE, the sharp bounds may not vary monotonically with the correlation, and we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for point identification of the LATE at any feasible correlation value, with the conventional Wald ratio identification result under monotonicity as a special case. In addition, we derive a breakdown point for the correlation that determines when the Wald ratio falls outside the sharp identified set for the LATE. Applications to four empirical studies illustrate how cross-world correlation restrictions tighten the sharp bounds for the ATE and LATE and assess the breakdown of the Wald ratio.
item.dc:creator: Zhaoqing Tian, Lin Liu, Yue Liu, Peng Wu

item.title: Model-Based Clustering of Longitudinal Functional Data with Hidden Semi-Markov Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.32693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model-based clustering of longitudinal functional data must account both for heterogeneity among curves and for temporal dependence in their latent group memberships. Functional mixture models typically treat curves as exchangeable, while temporal approaches may restrict regime persistence or ignore state-specific functional variation. We propose hidden semi-Markov models for ordered sequences of multivariate functional observations in which each latent regime has a parsimonious, state-specific functional principal subspace, extending functional high-dimensional data clustering (funHDDC) to longitudinal settings. Gaussian, contaminated-Gaussian and multivariate-$t$ emissions accommodate atypical observations, and explicit state-specific sojourn distributions govern regime persistence, with hidden Markov models as the geometric special case. Estimation uses expectation-maximization (EM) and expectation/conditional-maximization (ECM) algorithms with segmental forward-backward recursions, and identifiability is established up to label permutations and spectral indeterminacies. In simulations, temporal dependence yields the largest gains when single curves are weakly informative; with robust emissions, state-specific subspaces outperform a global functional principal component representation; and explicit durations add smaller gains when regimes overlap and sojourns are non-geometric. Applications to air-quality profiles and smartphone activity recordings, evaluated on held-out years and subjects, show improved predictive fit and illustrate how apparent duration effects can reflect time-varying transitions.
item.dc:creator: Bagas Caesar Suherlan, Emilio Porcu, Antonello Maruotti

item.title: Regression calibration for logistic regression with correlated measurement error and multiple misclassification in covariates
item.description: arXiv:2611.32878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Epidemiological analyses often suffer from covariate data quality issues: measurement error in continuous predictors and misclassification of categorical variables. Existing logistic regression correction methods mostly handle only one error type or a single misclassified variable, with limited tools for multiple misclassified categorical exposures together with correlated measurement error in continuous covariates. To address this gap, we extend regression calibration for logistic regression to jointly accommodate multiple continuous covariates with correlated additive measurement error and two or more misclassified categorical predictors. We build a unified framework integrating additive measurement error models and misclassification transition matrices, deriving the regression calibration estimator (RCE) using Kronecker product algebra. This computationally feasible approach extends naturally to more than two misclassified categorical variables. We evaluate RCE via simulations across varied misclassification rates, error magnitudes, sample sizes and effect sizes, comparing it with the naive estimator that ignores measurement error. We apply RCE to the EPIC-InterAct male case-cohort data to adjust for correlated error in protein and energy intake, plus misclassification in binary physical activity and three-category alcohol consumption. Results show that neglecting these error sources produces substantial bias and misleading inference for main and interaction effects in nutritional epidemiology. While the RCE is a practical correction tool, it treats validation nuisance parameters as known and does not account for their estimation uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Zhiqiang Cao, Man Yu Wong

item.title: Generalizing Couple-Randomized Trials Under Limited Overlap and Missing Partner Linkage
item.description: arXiv:2611.32888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how to generalize couple-randomized trials when some couple types are absent from the trial and the target survey reports partner characteristics without linking spouses. Under an additive effect model with unrestricted partner-profile terms, the target average effect is identified exactly when the wife and husband margins assign equal mass to each connected component of the trial support graph. A specified interaction is identified when its alternating contrast around at least one cycle is nonzero. Without linkage, we obtain sharp bounds by optimizing over pairings consistent with the survey margins. A spousal odds ratio can narrow the bounds for a binary interaction. We derive joint bounds for an index-patient design, quantify bias from common shortcuts, and estimate effects and bounds using Bayesian dyadic multilevel regression and poststratification. In a worked example based on 3,826 Health and Retirement Study couples and simulated trial outcomes, an index-patient trial and an unlinked survey yielded a 2.93 mmHg wide identified set for the couple-average effect. Linking the survey narrowed it to 2.38 mmHg. Adding 300 couples without diabetes narrowed the unlinked set to 0.28 mmHg and yielded point identification with linkage under the fitted model.
item.dc:creator: Subir Hait

item.title: Statistical Process Monitoring of Functional Linear Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.32936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monitoring the stability over time of the relationship between a functional response and multiple functional covariates is important in many industrial applications, either because the relationship itself is the quality characteristic of interest or because it underpins a predictive model whose validity must be verified as the process evolves. Existing methods either assume the model estimated in Phase I to be stable and monitor the resulting residuals, or re-estimate its coefficients at each sampling stage, which requires several observations to be available at a time. In this article, we propose the regression coefficient function (RCF) control chart to monitor functional linear models (FLMs) in which, at each sampling stage, an individual observation of the functional response and an arbitrary number of functional covariates become available. The proposed method employs an exponentially weighted moving loss to sequentially update estimates of the regression coefficient functions and the intercept function, which are monitored through Hotelling's $T^2$ and squared prediction error (SPE) control charts. A post-signal diagnostic procedure is also provided to support the identification of the source of the detected change. A Monte Carlo simulation study demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly against small and persistent shifts, and a case study on monitoring the relationship between the air/fuel ratio and engine state variables in an automotive after-treatment system illustrates its practical applicability.
item.dc:creator: Davide Forcina, Antonio Lepore, Kamran Paynabar

item.title: Certifying total-variation contamination by betting on trimmed kernel witnesses
item.description: arXiv:2611.33039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two laws share a common component after each discards a fraction $\alpha$ of its mass, a trimming, exactly when their total variation is at most $\alpha$, so the contamination level $\alpha^\star = \mathrm{TV} (P,Q)$ is the share of each population without counterpart in the other. We bound it from below from two samples on any space with a bounded characteristic kernel. The kernel mean embeddings of all such trimmings of a law form a convex region, the regions of two laws first touch at $\alpha^\star$, and in every direction a region reaches as far as a trimmed mean. The difference of their closest points, the witness, selects the trimming. We fit a ramp of the witness on part of the data and bet on the rest, at each level of a grid. The bound is valid at every sample size. The cut points of the tested level carry most of its finite-sample gain over an untrimmed witness, while refitting the witness at that level makes it consistent, gives its rates and returns the trimming. When a function of the kernel's Hilbert space separates the parts of the two laws without counterpart, the bound is within order $(n\wedge m)^{-1/2}$ of $\alpha^\star$ on a grid of that mesh, which is minimax over such pairs. When these parts touch, a margin condition guarantees a polynomial rate for Sobolev kernels and a logarithmic rate for the Gaussian kernel. For the Laplace kernel on the line this guarantee is not sharp: the witness stays between its two cut points, and for densities that cross once, with a likelihood ratio bounded away from one off the crossing, the error on such a grid is again of that order up to logarithmic factors. No informative upper bound exists without assumptions. On the Right Heart Catheterization data, with confidence $0.95$, each arm must lose more than a fraction $0.35$ of its patients, if both lose the same fraction, before their covariate distributions can coincide.
item.dc:creator: Hristo Inouzhe Valdes

item.title: Bayesian Learning of Spatially Heterogeneous Causal Structure in Spatial Transcriptomics
item.description: arXiv:2611.33094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics preserves the location of each expression profile, making it possible to study how gene regulatory networks differ within a tissue. Across regions of a tissue, regulatory relationships may vary and even reverse direction, so identifying the causal relationships in a specific pathological region can provide insight into therapeutic targets. We propose SpaDAG, a Bayesian method for learning spatially varying causal directed acyclic graphs. By defining the graphs on a triangulation of the tissue, SpaDAG allows each edge to have its own spatial pattern and even to reverse direction across regions. We show that the graphs nonetheless remain fully identifiable, and develop an MCMC sampler that explores them efficiently by reversing an edge over an entire connected region in a single move. SpaDAG outperforms competing methods in simulations with and without direction reversals. In a section spanning a renal cell carcinoma and the adjacent kidney, SpaDAG finds largely different relationships in the two tissues, with those in the tumor concentrated on genes associated with therapeutic targets. Between two of these genes, it identifies a relationship whose direction reverses across the tumor boundary, generating hypotheses about their region-specific coupling. Supplementary materials and code for this article are available online.
item.dc:creator: Kyungwook Back, Junsouk Choi

item.title: Local subspace encoding for spectral prediction: from TabPFN to operator-adaptive calibration
item.description: arXiv:2611.31245v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: TabPFN has already shown useful predictive performance on near-infrared spectra. RamanPFN subsequently proposed two spectral representations for tabular inference: Global Compositional Unmixing (GCU) and Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding (LVSE). We assess whether these representations also help on datasets assembled through the nirs4all ecosystem, and whether their value extends to classical calibration. We reanalyse completed experiments from a public spectral dataset catalogue. On a post-hoc subset of 61 matched numerical prediction tasks, after excluding ten class-code, metadata or semantically ambiguous targets, LVSE reduces RMSE relative to raw-spectrum TabPFN by 10.22%, 12.80% and 14.52% on average for checkpoints 2.5, 3 and 3.5, respectively, with median reductions of 4.99%, 4.74% and 7.82%. Across 76 classification datasets, weighted F1 increases by 2.22, 2.56 and 3.81 percentage points. The 2.5 classification procedure uses output coding on 15 datasets exceeding the checkpoint's native class limit. GCU alone is less reliable in this implementation. LVSE also improves PLS and Ridge in many cases, with median RMSE reductions of 4.75% and 1.89%. Adding LVSE candidates to an operator-adaptive model is feasible, but a separate 35-task panel derived from the public AOM benchmark shows only small median gains. These results motivate evaluating LVSE alongside existing representation choices. They do not establish that a selector choosing between raw and LVSE inputs will improve every task.
item.dc:creator: Gregory Beurier, Robin Reiter, Denis Cornet, Lauriane Rouan

item.title: Agent Evaluation Without Ground Truth: A Null Proportion Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2611.31539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The correctness of actions taken by agents is typically evaluated against known, externally verified ground truth labels, such as whether a proof is correct or whether code compiles and passes unit tests. However, as coding and science agents are entrusted with more end-to-end autonomy -- proposing interventions, running experiments, and deciding what to deploy and investigate next -- whether an agent's actions genuinely improve an outcome must be inferred from noisy, often inconclusive experiments. To evaluate agents in this setting, we define agent quality as a weighted sum of correct decisions along its trajectory, using sequences of $e$-values as statistical evidence regarding correctness in place of ground-truth labels. Our framework accommodates arbitrarily dependent decisions, data-dependent trajectory termination, dynamically generated hypotheses, and quality measures defined after the trajectory concludes. We construct upper and lower bound estimators and confidence sets for agent quality with statistical guarantees that hold uniformly over agent trajectory distributions and establish instance-wise sharpness of our estimator class. We demonstrate our methods with a case study comparing the success of Claude Opus and Claude Haiku in improving the runtime of an open-source Python package.
item.dc:creator: Brian M. Cho, Michael Lindon, Nathan Kallus

item.title: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.31595v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cheap language-model raters grade chain-of-thought reasoning at scale, yet systematic step-rating errors can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. We introduce LUCID (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis), which pairs prompt self-correction with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL). Without retraining or weight access, LUCID calibrates binary step ratings by aligning predicted and expert soundness rates. From a small expert-labeled set, LUCID summarizes rater bias in plain text and prompts the rater to re-grade unseen steps. For example, on PRM800K, GPT-5-mini grades too strictly, under-rating computation, verification, and late-trace steps most acutely. In one pass, LUCID shrinks GPT-5-mini's calibration gap from 7.8 to 0.9 percentage points in absolute predicted-expert rate difference. LUCID also halves false alarms (sound steps rated unsound) and lifts error-detection F1 on unsound steps by 32%. LUCID retains these gains with 1,000 diagnostic steps or overall-gap feedback alone. The loop also transfers across models and domains: it applies GPT-5-mini's bias profile to lift GLM-5.2's PRM800K accuracy, and it narrows calibration gaps for overly strict but capable raters across math, science, web, and logic benchmarks. Because prompt feedback shifts thresholds without improving class-balanced sound/unsound discrimination, LUCID filters re-grading with pre-/post-checks that skip already calibrated raters and roll back ineffective passes. Finally, we reuse that expert set with raw corpus ratings in DSL for calibration and regression debiasing, and apply DSL to pair-labeled steps for sound-step transitions. DSL's out-of-fold soundness probabilities lift best-of-K selection to match expert labels, while its doubly-robust estimators beat expert-only regression fits at small budgets and cut sound-step transition error by nearly two-thirds.
item.dc:creator: Satiyabooshan Murugaboopathy, Adel Daoud, Connor T. Jerzak

item.title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.31619v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier
item.dc:creator: Arya Sikder, Sriram Pillutla

item.title: An entropy-adjusted invariant likelihood for incidental parameters
item.description: arXiv:2611.31707v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Incidental parameters can make maximum likelihood inconsistent in short panels. When they act through a known translation group, integration with respect to Haar measure eliminates them exactly and gives an invariant likelihood, whose score is shown to be the conditional expectation, given the maximal invariant, of the Neyman-orthogonalised score of every order. Under interactive fixed effects the orbit is an unknown factor space, and the invariant score for it has a drift equal to minus the derivative of the entropy of the retained contrasts. An entropy adjustment removes this drift and, at the true structural parameter, identifies the factor space uniquely when the loadings span it. The adjusted estimating equations are the gradient of a single criterion if and only if the entropy separates into an orbit term and an error-law term, as in scale and elliptical families; consistency then follows from a design condition, and in general from an equilibrium-identification condition, with asymptotic normality for fixed panel length. A boundary is derived for recovering a skewness sign discarded by a two-period invariant reduction. An application to Vietnamese rice farming rejects equal household-effect weights across survey waves and finds lower returns to scale.
item.dc:creator: Xibin Zhang

item.title: Sharp Hellinger Risk of the Multivariate Gaussian NPMLE
item.description: arXiv:2611.31728v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For multivariate Gaussian location mixtures whose mixing distributions have coordinatewise sub-Gaussian tails, we prove that the unconstrained nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator attains the minimax rate $(\log n)^d/n$ under squared Hellinger loss. This holds for every fixed dimension $d\geq2$ and every fixed tail parameter $\sigma>0$. The upper bound applies to every measurable choice of a global likelihood maximizer and improves the earlier bound of order $(\log n)^{d+1}/n$ by a factor of $\log n$. A key step is a sharp bracketing bound for multivariate polynomials. For the $L^2(\rho)$ unit ball of real polynomials in $d$ variables with total degree at most $m$, the log bracketing number at width $\varepsilon$ is at most $\binom{m+d}{d}\log(C_d/\varepsilon)$ for $0<\varepsilon\leq1$. The constant $C_d$ depends only on $d$. The bound holds for every positive Borel measure $\rho$ under which each nonzero polynomial in the space has a finite, positive $L^2(\rho)$ norm. We prove the bound using volume estimates for a complex Veronese cone and Gaussian small-ball probabilities, then apply it to bound the local Hellinger bracketing entropy of Gaussian mixture densities. We obtain the matching minimax lower bound by adapting the Hermite perturbation construction of Kim and Guntuboyina.
item.dc:creator: Xingzhou Wang, Zheng Li

item.title: Asymptotic Normality of the Pearson Correlation between Two Weakly Dependent Random Fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.31743v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior of the sample Pearson correlation coefficient between two weakly dependent random fields on a lattice of any fixed dimension. Under strict stationarity, $(BL,\theta)$-weak dependence and mild moment conditions, we establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimator on regularly growing domains, which need not be rectangular, with an asymptotic variance expressed through joint fourth-order moments. When the correlation is zero, asymptotic normality holds under weaker conditions. When the fields are independent, the asymptotic variance simplifies to a sum over spatial lags of products of their autocorrelations. The variance approximations behind the classic modified $t$-test, although derived for independent Gaussian fields, target the right variance even without Gaussianity. We also give sufficient conditions for asymptotic normality that are easy to check and cover bounded, Gaussian, $m$-dependent and independent fields. For Gaussian fields, summable auto- and cross-covariances suffice. These conditions rely on new closure results. Squares and products, although not Lipschitz, preserve $(BL,\theta)$-dependence for Gaussian fields, and products of independent fields do so when one is positively or negatively associated. Finally, we propose kernel-based estimators of the asymptotic variance, enabling inference without Gaussianity or parametric spatial models. Simulation studies illustrate their finite-sample performance.
item.dc:creator: Jiyue Qin, Armin Schwartzman, Samuel Davenport

item.title: A General Framework for E-process Stopping Rules in Best-Arm Identification
item.description: arXiv:2611.31898v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose an e-process stopping rule in the best-arm identification problem. The e-process stopping rule is different from the Chernoff stopping rule by its hypothesis structure on the stopping decision. The major benefit of an e-process stopping rule is the flexibility in stopping rule design and in fact, it recovers previously suggested Chernoff stopping rule on several bandit problems. Moreover, we analyze the asymptotic optimality of the $\delta$-PAC algorithm with the decomposition of e-processes. The decomposition separates optimality conditions into three parts; the sampling policy allocation convergence, the efficiency of e-process design, and the bandit problem's inherent stochastic behavior. Subsequently, we prove a sufficient condition for asymptotic optimality in bandit algorithms. For the application of an e-process stopping rule, we derived an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the generalized linear bandit problem.
item.dc:creator: Donghyun Park, Seohwa Hwang, Junyong Park

item.title: A General Framework for Identifying the Joint Potential Outcome Distribution through Support Restrictions
item.description: arXiv:2611.31900v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many causal estimands depend on the joint distribution of potential outcomes, which is generally not identifiable because only one potential outcome can be observed for each unit. To obtain identification, researchers often impose assumptions such as monotonicity and exclusion restriction that constrain the support of this joint distribution. For treatments and outcomes that each take finitely many values, we define a similarity matrix whose entries count, for each pair of potential outcome strata, the number of treatments yielding the same outcome. We then prove that, under unconfoundedness, identification holds if and only if this matrix is invertible, yielding a criterion directly verifiable from the support. In addition, we derive an identification formula for the joint distribution under these support restrictions and show that an average causal estimand is identifiable if and only if its integrand admits an additive representation on the restricted support. Finally, we derive sharp testable implications of the support restriction. Our results unify and generalize a broad range of identification results in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Benedikt Koch, Kosuke Imai

item.title: Meta-Amortized Cognitive Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.31914v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cognitive modeling is highly iterative. Researchers repeatedly revise model structures, parameterizations, covariates, and experimental designs as theories evolve and data accumulates. Amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks provides rapid estimation for individual models, but every revision requires new simulations and training. Here, we introduce CogFormerV2, a meta-amortized framework that enables researchers to specify, revise, and fit cognitive models with a single network, carrying amortization across an entire space of models all at once. Trained once in about a day on a single GPU, it delivers accurate, well-calibrated posteriors across more than 14.6 billion model configurations spanning binary, multi-alternative, and continuous decisions, with varying parameter sets, covariate structures, trial counts, and contamination levels. It can fit empirical data from distinct behavioral tasks and extends to new models through continual learning and representation transfer. Released as an open-source interactive application, CogFormerV2 provides a reusable infrastructure for meta-amortized inference in cognitive modeling, while carrying the potential to accelerate computational modeling workflows at large.
item.dc:creator: Jerry M. Huang, Lukas Schumacher, Niek Stevenson, Mischa von Krause, Stefan T. Radev

item.title: Structure-Aware Transformers for Hierarchical Authorization in Personal AI Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.32018v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Personal AI agents can carry out complex, multi-step tasks on users' behalf, but doing so often involves numerous permission requests. Manually reviewing each request is time-consuming, while indiscriminate approval poses privacy and security risks. Predicting users' authorization preferences offers a way to reduce this burden while preserving user control. However, authorization prediction is challenging because permission requests are often hierarchical and observed user decisions are sparse and potentially correlated. To address these challenges, We propose the Parent-gated Authorization Transformer for Hierarchies (PATH) to predict users' authorization preferences for personal AI agents. PATH is a novel neural network architecture that combines hierarchy-aware attention masks with a parent-gated probability formulation to ensure hierarchy-consistent predictions. Hierarchy-level embeddings further support learning from sparse observations and patterns shared within each authorization level. We establish finite-sample risk bounds and provide sufficient conditions for consistent authorization probability estimation and algorithmic convergence. Experiments on simulated data, AI-generated user profiles, and real user authorization data demonstrate strong predictive performance with zero hierarchy violations.
item.dc:creator: Dongyu Cui, Jie Ding, Xuan Bi

item.title: Admissibility of Linear Time Series Models under Cone Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.32414v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Time series analysis extends beyond vector-valued observations to evolving probability densities, quantile functions, and covariance operators. These objects carry intrinsic constraints, raising questions about the admissibility of additive linear models, which have long served as a foundation for time series modelling and theory. We give a necessary and sufficient support condition for a stationary Hilbert-space linear process to remain in a closed convex cone almost surely. Innovations with unbounded lower tails, including Gaussian innovations, confine randomness to the cone's largest linear subspace. For fractional filters with convergent normalized cumulative coefficients, the leading stochastic directions obey the same restriction, even with bounded innovations. For real-line quantiles, variation under unbounded lower tails and leading fractional accumulation can occur only through location shifts. For cone-valued processes, partial sums of centred stationary increments remain bounded in mean square when evaluated by any linear functional that is nonnegative on the cone, in contrast to the growing variance of a random walk. We derive an exact slope criterion for locally absolutely continuous quantiles and construct nondegenerate additive models with bounded innovations for quantiles, densities, and covariance matrices. These findings clarify the scope of ordinary additive modelling under structural constraints.
item.dc:creator: Won-Ki Seo

item.title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.32430v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many real-world interactions involve groups of nodes rather than pairs. A non-uniform hypergraph records such interactions as hyperedges of different orders, where the order counts the nodes in a hyperedge. Full estimation evaluates every candidate hyperedge, whose number grows exponentially with the order, and classical remedies sacrifice higher-order information or aggravate computation. The orders are not isolated: the lower orders, cheap to compute and rich in information, reveal where higher-order hyperedges are likely to occur. We propose CINE (Cross-order Information-guided Negative-sampling Estimation) under a latent space model in which all orders share latent positions. Starting from order two, CINE climbs one order at a time. At each higher order, CINE keeps all present hyperedges, samples a small subset of negative examples guided by lower-order scores, and corrects for the known inclusion probabilities to preserve the target of full estimation. CINE thereby lets users choose the trade-off between computation time and estimation accuracy: the retained orders and the sampling budget set the time, and the retained information provably approaches full-data information as the sampling budget grows. In simulations, CINE approaches the accuracy of full estimation at a small fraction of its computation time, and larger teams in MADStat reveal research associations.
item.dc:creator: Rongzhuo Nie, Menghao Wang, Sanguo Zhang, Mingyang Ren, Guojun Zhu

item.title: Adaptive Multi-kernel Correntropy Kalman Filter: A Variational Bayesian Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.32679v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper proposes an adaptive multi-kernel correntropy Kalman filter (AMCKF) for robust state estimation in the presence of heavy-tailed measurement noises and outliers. The multi-kernel correntropy loss is reformulated via half-quadratic (HQ) duality into a quadratic form with auxiliary weights, enabling efficient Kalman-like recursions. We establish a rigorous variational Bayesian framework under the mean-field assumption, deriving closed-form coordinate ascent variational inference updates for joint state and kernel width estimation. To enable online implementation, AMCKF is then proposed as an efficient single-pass approximation of the exact coordinate ascent variational inference (CAVI), where the state and auxiliary variables are updated iteratively via IRLS, followed by a closed-form kernel width update. A forgetting mechanism is designed to prevent over-confidence and ensure long-term adaptability. Simulations on target tracking and IMU attitude estimation demonstrate that the proposed AMCKF significantly outperforms standard KF, VBKF, Student's t-based KF, and fixed-kernel MKCKF in scenarios with sparse outliers, heavy-tailed noise, and mixed disturbances, while maintaining optimal performance under Gaussian conditions.
item.dc:creator: Zhen Zeng, Shilei Li, Dawei Shi, Ling Shi

item.title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores
item.description: arXiv:2611.32792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The internal activations of modern machine learning models align surprisingly well with the activities recorded in real brains. In the last five years, the alignment between encoding models and brain activities, often called brain scores, has steadily increased. Because brain recordings are noisy, there exists an upper bound to the brain scores that any model can achieve. This bound, called the noise ceiling, is crucial for two reasons: it determines whether further improvements in model performance are possible, and it enables meaningful comparisons of brain scores across benchmarks. The field has developed multiple approaches to estimate noise ceilings, but the statistical properties of existing estimators remain poorly understood, leaving it unclear in which experimental settings they provide reliable estimates. Here, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, use it to derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and provide theoretical predictions for the behavior of each estimator. We validate the theoretical predictions with simulations that we compare to noise ceiling estimates in existing fMRI and EEG datasets. We find that the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings. We conclude with recommendations for best practice in different situations.
item.dc:creator: Aude Maier, Lucas Gruaz, Martin Schrimpf, Johanni Brea

item.title: Efficient inferential models and their fiducial connections
item.description: arXiv:2611.32930v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Valid inferential models (IMs) provide frequentist calibration guarantees, but validity alone does not determine which construction is most informative. We study finite-sample efficiency through concentration risk, the expected volume under a possibility contour. For a smooth, fully identified association and a specified parameter-volume measure, a weighted Neyman--Pearson argument identifies the generalized fiducial density as the optimal score for minimizing cut volume subject to fixed-data auxiliary compatibility. The resulting maximum-specificity transform gives an explicit volume interpretation of the fiducial efficiency ceiling, which need not itself be sampling valid. We develop two approaches to valid construction. The first minimizes design-averaged concentration risk among single, data-independent auxiliary-compatible contours. The design measure prioritizes efficiency without requiring prior beliefs or restricting validity. The second localizes the parameter-volume score to candidate-specific contours, yielding a normalized, valid IM equivalent to sampling validification of the relative fiducial likelihood. A parallel sample-space construction recovers the ordinary likelihood-ratio IM; direct validification of the ceiling provides another repair. For the same association, exact, data-independent predictive contours share a common fiducial distribution as a saturating inner probability, while generating different calibrated confidence-region geometries. Design averaging thus selects an efficient member without changing the underlying fiducial law. Examples in a two-component measurement model and an exponential scale model illustrate the efficiency gains and show that sampling-valid repair can improve on the raw ceiling by leaving the fixed-data auxiliary-compatible class over which it is optimal.
item.dc:creator: Max Raner

item.title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32945v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clustering is a foundational tool for exploratory data analysis across the sciences. We argue that clustering methods should be evaluated along four dimensions: fidelity to the data's underlying structure, interpretability of the recovered groups, stability under data perturbations and algorithmic randomness, and scalability to modern scientific datasets. Yet existing methods rarely satisfy all four criteria. To address this gap, we introduce PHM-ensemble, a general probabilistic framework for multiresolution clustering that estimates the underlying data density by pooling mixture models from an ensemble of fits and subsequently constructs a clustering hierarchy through hierarchical merging of the mixture components. On simulated datasets and the MNIST benchmark, PHM-ensemble matches or outperforms widely used clustering algorithms in agreement with ground truth, produces more stable results across runs, and reveals complex underlying structures. Applied to 1.82 million peripheral blood cells from the Human Immune Health Atlas, PHM-ensemble achieves higher agreement with expert-curated major cell-type annotations than the Leiden clustering used in the original study (adjusted Rand index 0.965 versus 0.789), while requiring only half the computing time. Beyond identifying major immune lineages, it reveals biologically coherent relationships among cell types and resolves finer structure within individual lineages, uncovering subtypes and cellular states consistent with known biology.
item.dc:creator: Ali Turfah, Xiaoquan Wen

item.title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.32947v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are increasingly applied in mobile health (mHealth), where treatment decisions are made continually. Luckett et al. (2020) proposed V-learning, which estimates an optimal policy from offline trajectories. In practice, mHealth policies are updated online. Batch updating, in which the policy is re-estimated after each block of new data, is a tractable middle ground between offline learning and updating after every observation. However, because each batch's treatment policy is estimated from data pooled across patients in earlier batches, the resulting data are adaptively collected and patient trajectories are dependent, a setting that offline theory does not address. We develop statistical theory for V-learning in this setting with varying, deterministic batch sizes. For each fixed batch, as the number of patients grows, we establish uniform consistency of the estimated value function, consistency of the estimated policy, a functional central limit theorem over the policy class, asymptotic normality of the estimated value of the learned policy, and a consistent variance estimator. To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch. With the number of patients fixed and the number of batches growing, the estimated value function and policy remain consistent under a persistent identifiability condition. In simulations, as the number of patients grows with the number of batches fixed, confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage under adaptive assignment and the online procedure closely matches the oracle. With a small cohort followed over many batches, the learned policies improve steadily.
item.dc:creator: Aniruddhan Ganesaraman, Michael R. Kosorok

item.title: Pragmatic Deeply Debiased ML
item.description: arXiv:2611.33069v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Debiased machine learning (DML) combines a fitted outcome regression with weighted residuals to remove first-order regularization bias when estimating parameters such as average treatment effects, yet a second-order bias remains whenever regression and weighting errors align. For linear regression functionals, we target this second-order bias by training a strong learner to predict first-stage residuals from many covariates, yielding a one-dimensional (or low-dimensional) working model whose bias contribution is estimated on an independent sample. To complement this targeted search, we also analyze general kernel-based corrections, including covariate partitions and smoothers. We prove that deeply debiased ML is algebraically identical to ordinary DML evaluated with a post-hoc regression update that adjusts each scored observation using kernel-weighted residuals from the remaining evaluation observations. In our empirical and simulation studies, strong initial DML learners often leave the second-order correction small relative to sampling uncertainty, in which case the correction serves as a diagnostic check alongside sensitivity bounds for any remaining misspecification bias.
item.dc:creator: Victor Chernozhukov, Chengchun Shi

item.title: Measurement Errors in Semiparametric Generalized Regression Models
item.description: arXiv:2104.04190v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Regression models that ignore measurement error in predictors may produce highly biased estimates leading to erroneous inferences. It is well known that it is extremely difficult to take measurement error into account in Gaussian nonparametric regression. This problem becomes tremendously more difficult when considering other families such as logistic regression, Poisson and negative-binomial. For the first time, we present a method aiming to correct for measurement error when estimating regression functions flexibly covering virtually all distributions and link functions regularly considered in generalized linear models. This approach depends on approximating the first and the second moment of the response after integrating out the true unobserved predictors in a semiparametric generalized linear model. Unlike previous methods, this method is not restricted to truncated splines and can utilize various basis functions. Through extensive simulation studies, we study the performance of our method under many scenarios.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Statistics 65(4), 344-363 (2023)
item.dc:creator: Mohammad W. Hattab, David Ruppert

item.title: Treatment Effects in Extreme Regimes
item.description: arXiv:2306.11697v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding treatment effects in extreme regimes is important for characterizing risks associated with different interventions. This is hindered by the unavailability of counterfactual outcomes and the rarity and difficulty of collecting extreme data in practice. To address this issue, we propose a new framework based on extreme value theory for estimating treatment effects in extreme regimes. We quantify these effects using variations in tail decay rates of potential outcomes in the presence and absence of treatments. We establish algorithms for calculating these quantities and develop related theoretical results. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on various standard synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Aloui, Ali Hasan, Yuting Ng, Miroslav Pajic, Vahid Tarokh

item.title: Spatiotemporal Causal Inference with Spillover and Carryover Effects: Airstrikes and Insurgent Violence in Vietnam and Afghanistan
item.description: arXiv:2504.03464v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Do airstrikes suppress insurgent violence or provoke it? Answering such questions requires methods that preserve the spatial and temporal structure of airstrikes and insurgent retaliation. Yet nearly all microlevel research aggregates fine-grained data into panels built on large administrative units and long time intervals. This practice forecloses direct tests of causal mechanisms and imposes restrictive assumptions about spillover and carryover that bias estimates. We develop a practical framework for spatiotemporal causal inference in which treatment, mediator, and outcome all retain their precise locations and timing. Applying it to declassified airstrike data from Vietnam and Afghanistan, we find that bombing displaces, but does not suppress, insurgent violence. Insurgent retaliation follows predictable patterns, concentrating near rebel-controlled hamlets (Vietnam) and U.S. bases (Afghanistan) and emerging about a week later. Civilian harm does not mediate this response. Post-airstrike insurgent violence appears less about avenging aggrieved civilians than demonstrating resolve by imposing costs on counterinsurgents.
item.dc:creator: Mitsuru Mukaigawara, Kosuke Imai, Jason Lyall, Georgia Papadogeorgou

item.title: Sequential Monte Carlo approximations of Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao gradient flows
item.description: arXiv:2506.05905v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the problem of sampling from a probability distribution $\pi$. It is well known that this can be written as an optimisation problem over the space of probability distribution in which we aim to minimise the Kullback--Leibler divergence from $\pi$. We consider several partial differential equations (PDEs) whose solution is a minimiser of the Kullback--Leibler divergence from $\pi$ and connect them to well-known Monte Carlo algorithms. We focus in particular on PDEs obtained by considering the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry over the space of probabilities and show that these lead to a natural implementation using importance sampling and sequential Monte Carlo. We propose a novel algorithm to approximate the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao flow of the Kullback--Leibler divergence and conduct an extensive empirical study to identify when this algorithm outperforms other popular Monte Carlo algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Francesca R. Crucinio, Sahani Pathiraja

item.title: Statistical Inference for Fuzzy Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2601.02656v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Clustering is a central tool in biomedical research for discovering heterogeneous patient subpopulations, where group boundaries are often diffuse rather than sharply separated. While soft clustering methods such as fuzzy $c$-means (FCM) allow mixed memberships, principled statistical inference for fuzzy clustering remains limited. We propose a weighted fuzzy $c$-means (WFCM) framework for settings with cluster-size imbalance. Cluster-specific weights $\mathbf{w}$ re-balance the classic FCM criterion to adjust the relative influence of clusters of unequal size, and we construct a normalized working density from the weighted objective with scale parameter $\sigma$ and fuzziness parameter $m$. Estimation is performed via FCM-style alternating initialization followed by numerical likelihood refinement; the intractable normalizing constant is approximated by importance sampling using a data-adaptive Gaussian-mixture as the proposal distribution. We further develop bootstrap-based confidence intervals. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, validate the method in simulations, and illustrate it on single-cell RNA-seq, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), and TCGA-BRCA data. These applications illustrate uncertainty quantification and interpretable soft memberships, ranging from imbalanced cell populations to graded compatibility with AD-like and non-AD-like prototypes.
item.dc:creator: Qiuyi Wu, Zihan Zhu, Anru R. Zhang

item.title: Deriving Complete Constraints in Hidden Variable Models
item.description: arXiv:2601.11242v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hidden variable graphical models can sometimes imply constraints on the observable distribution that are more complex than simple conditional independence relations. These observable constraints can falsify assumptions of the model and can be used to constrain estimation procedures to improve statistical efficiency. Knowing the complete set of observable constraints is thus ideal, but this can be difficult to determine in many settings. In models with categorical observed variables and a joint distribution that is completely characterized by linear relations to the probabilities of unobservable response function variables, we develop a systematic method for deriving the complete set of observable constraints. We illustrate the method in several settings, including ones that imply both inequality and equality constraints.
item.dc:creator: Michael C. Sachs, Erin E. Gabriel, Robin J. Evans, Arvid Sj\"olander

item.title: Flexible Matrix Estimation with Side Information
item.description: arXiv:2603.24833v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a flexible framework for high-dimensional matrix estimation to incorporate side information for both rows and columns. Existing approaches, such as inductive matrix completion, often impose restrictive structure---for example, an exact low-rank covariate interaction term, linear covariate effects, and limited ability to exploit components explained only by one side (row or column) or by neither---and frequently omit an explicit noise component. To address these limitations, we propose to decompose the underlying matrix as the sum of four complementary components: (possibly nonlinear) interaction between row and column characteristics; row characteristic-driven component, column characteristic-driven component, and residual low-rank structure unexplained by observed characteristics. By combining sieve-based projection with nuclear-norm penalization, each component can be estimated separately and these estimated components can then be aggregated to yield a final estimate. We derive Frobenius- and entrywise-norm convergence rates that demonstrate the robustness of our estimator across a broad range of model configurations with varying degrees of informativeness in the side information. We further extend the method to partially observed matrices under both missing-at-random and missing-not-at-random mechanisms, including block-missing patterns motivated by causal panel data. Simulations and a real-data application to tobacco sales show that leveraging side information improves imputation accuracy and can enhance treatment-effect estimation relative to standard low-rank and spectral-based alternatives.
item.dc:creator: Anish Agarwal, Jungjun Choi, Ming Yuan

item.title: Generalized win fraction regression for composite survival endpoints
item.description: arXiv:2604.04360v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a generalized win fraction regression framework for prioritized composite survival outcomes. The framework models the conditional win fraction through a chosen link function (including identity, logit, or probit), thereby accommodating multi-component time-to-event endpoints within a unified regression structure. To handle right censoring, we construct inverse-probability-of-censoring-weighted estimating equations that target the win fraction as if censoring were absent. Under the identity link, regression parameters characterize covariate associations on the natural win fraction scale. Under the logit link, they characterize the log odds of winning -- a new and complementary effect measure that treats ties as failures to win, imposing a more conservative standard than the win ratio or win odds. When there are no ties, the logit win fraction model reduces to proportional win fraction regression; moreover, the unweighted version of our estimating equations numerically coincides with the proportional win fraction point estimator regardless of ties. We establish large-sample properties of the proposed estimators and derive a consistent sandwich variance estimator that accounts for uncertainty from the estimated censoring weights. Extensive simulations examine finite-sample performance across link functions and censoring rates, and our method is illustrated through a reanalysis of the HF-ACTION clinical trial.
item.dc:creator: Zhiqiang Cao, Xi Fang, Fan Li

item.title: A Tutorial for Evaluating Cure Model Appropriateness
item.description: arXiv:2605.04999v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In survival analysis, traditional models assume all individuals will eventually experience the event of interest. However, advances in therapeutics have led to multiple clinical contexts with potentially curative therapies, and in these contexts, certain individuals may never experience the event. Statisticians have developed cure models as a methodology to address this challenge. However, despite significant statistical advances in cure models, we have seen more limited uptake in biomedical applications, and we hypothesize that this reflects limited guidance on the appropriate application of cure models. Cure models require specific identifiability conditions for valid parameter estimation, and previous reports have demonstrated significant issues with the inappropriate application of cure models. Existing tutorials for cure models focus on model implementation and either assume or provide only limited guidance on whether cure modeling is appropriate for the given dataset. This tutorial addresses this gap by describing a systematic procedure that integrates clinical judgment, visual inspection of Kaplan-Meier curves, and quantitative evaluation. We provide a worked example using data from a randomized clinical trial in acute myeloid leukemia, and we also summarize findings from a series of other datasets of hematopoietic cell transplantation to suggest broad practical guidance for choosing to apply cure models. By systematically evaluating cure model appropriateness before fitting these models, researchers can achieve more reliable survival analysis and improved clinical decision-making.
item.dc:creator: Geethanjalee Mudunkotuwa, Durbadal Ghosh, Subodh Selukar

item.title: Compensator-Based Inference for Signal Detection Under Unknown Background
item.description: arXiv:2605.20508v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The problem of detecting new signals in the presence of an unknown background is ubiquitous in scientific discoveries and is especially prominent in the physical sciences. Most solutions proposed thus far to address the problem focus on estimating the background distribution and using that estimate to infer the signal. By studying the geometry of the problem, this article demonstrates that estimating the background distribution is somewhat unnecessary for inferring the signal intensity. Instead, it suffices to estimate a single parameter, referred to as the compensator, to account for the incomplete knowledge of the background, substantially reducing the problem's complexity and enabling proper uncertainty propagation. Such a compensator is shown to govern the conservativeness of the inference, both in the proposed setup and in likelihood-based approaches.
item.dc:creator: Aritra Banerjee, Sara Algeri

item.title: Robust and Sparse Group Dynamic Causal Modeling via Student-t Parametric Empirical Bayes and Nonlocal Priors
item.description: arXiv:2609.06379v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) estimates directed effective connectivity, while parametric empirical Bayes (PEB) supports group inference using subject-specific posterior summaries. Standard PEB relies on Gaussian models and continuous shrinkage, making it sensitive to atypical estimates and unable to distinguish negligible from nonzero effects. We develop a robust and sparse group-DCM extension combining a Student-$t$ likelihood with a spike-and-slab prior using a nonlocal product-moment (pMOM) slab. A normal--gamma representation of the Student-$t$ distribution yields weights that downweight atypical {whitened residual coordinates}. The pMOM slab vanishes at zero, sharpening coefficient selection and yielding inclusion probabilities. {We propagate first-level posterior uncertainty through block-covariance pre-whitening and use a multistart generalized expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm with conditional maximization for mode fitting, followed by parallel-tempering posterior integration for inclusion probabilities. A simulation study showed that Student-$t$ weighting supplied the main protection against contamination, while spike-and-slab regularization reduced fixed-threshold false selections. In an openly shared mixed-gambles fMRI application, we found mild heterogeneity, concentrated inclusion support on departures of all four diagonal self-inhibition scaling parameters from the SPM default, and close directional agreement with standard PEB implemented in Statistical Parametric Mapping.} Our framework therefore adds interpretable {whitened-coordinate} robustness diagnostics and sparse coefficient selection to hierarchical DCM while retaining first-level uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Godfred Arhin, Nilotpal Sanyal

item.title: Exponential Smoothing for Time Series of Random Objects
item.description: arXiv:2609.20274v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time series of random objects, such as covariance matrices, probability distributions, and functional data, call for forecasting methods that do not rely on arithmetic operations. We introduce geodesic exponential smoothing for time series in Hadamard spaces. The forecast level moves a fixed fraction of the way along the geodesic towards each new observation. The smoothing parameter is estimated by minimising the average squared distance between observations and forecasts. The method involves a single scalar parameter, assumes no stationarity, and updates online in constant time per observation. We further introduce an innovations mechanism under which each observation has conditional Fr\'echet mean equal to the current level, the metric-space analogue of the innovations state-space model. We show via the quasilinearisation of Hadamard spaces that the level is a martingale in a nonlinear sense, that the spread of the data from the initial state grows at least linearly in time, and that their quasi-autocorrelation at any fixed lag tends to one. We prove almost-sure consistency and asymptotic normality of the smoothing-parameter estimator. Three real-data applications, spanning covariance-matrix, distributional, and functional time series, assess the forecasting performance against structurally heavier alternatives.
item.dc:creator: Takuo Matsubara, Peiwen Jiang, Wilson Ye Chen, Minh-Ngoc Tran

item.title: Anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test by $e$-spacings
item.description: arXiv:2611.23775v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To perform an anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test, we propose spacing-based $e$-processes that control the type-I error rate under arbitrary stopping rules. Based on the maximum spacing of order statistics, we construct spacing-based $e$-processes for nonparametrically testing distribution. The resulting procedures are simple and computationally efficient, and are power-consistent. We call them $e$-spacing tests. This approach is especially powerful in detecting localized discrepancy between the data-generating density and the null density. Under mild conditions, the logarithm of the proposed $e$-process is asymptotically equivalent to that of the oracle-optimal $e$-process. We further generalize the construction from maximal spacing to maximum spacing set in the form of the $1/k$ fraction of the largest $m$th order spacings, as a measure of the lower-level set of density. It boosts power under more global discrepancy from the null. Furthermore, we propose a greedy predictable scheme, via argmax or softmax rules, to combine multiple $e$-spacing testing strategies. We prove that it optimally tunes the $e$-spacing test. The proposed approach is readily generalizable to multivariate testing via a coordinate-wise Rosenblatt-transform. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably relative to the considered anytime-valid competitors as well as various types of multiple test-adjusted Kolmogorov--Smirnov tests.
item.dc:creator: Yunda Hao, Kin Wai Chan

item.title: $K$-Midranks: A robust clustering algorithm for heavy-tailed data with applications to spectroscopy and finance
item.description: arXiv:2611.30953v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Clustering data with extreme observations and heavy tails can be challenging for methods that rely on distances between raw observations or specific distributional assumptions. We introduce $K$-midranks, a clustering method that replaces observations with coordinatewise ranks and partitions the transformed data using a procedure analogous to $K$-means. This transformation reduces the influence of extreme values while preserving the ordering of observations within each variable. We evaluate $K$-midranks against $K$-means, $K$-medoids, and mixture models based on Gaussian, Student's t, Cauchy, and generalized hyperbolic distributions through simulation studies, and provide some theoretical properties. $K$-midranks generally outperforms the competing methods on Cauchy-shifted data. In contrast, $K$-means and model-based methods perform better on Gaussian data and Student's t data with three degrees of freedom. We demonstrate the method's practical use in grouping samples based on Raman and LIBS spectra and clustering S\&P 500 stocks according to their returns. $K$-midranks achieves competitive performance with model-based methods in the spectroscopy applications and the best performance among the methods considered in the stock-return application. These findings suggest that $K$-midranks provides a useful alternative for clustering data with Cauchy-like heavy tails. An R package implementing the proposed method is available.
item.dc:creator: Larry Goldstein, Nathakhun Wiroonsri

item.title: On importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings with an unbounded weight function
item.description: arXiv:2411.09514v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings are among the fundamental building blocks of Monte Carlo methods. Both require a proposal distribution that globally approximates the target distribution, and pointwise evaluation of the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the target distribution relative to the proposal, also called the weight function. We study the bias of importance sampling and independent Metropolis-Hastings, without assuming that the weight function is bounded. We show that the common random numbers coupling of independent Metropolis-Hastings is maximal. Using that coupling, we derive polynomial bounds on the total variation distance of the chain to its target distribution. We further consider bias removal techniques using couplings, and provide conditions under which the resulting unbiased estimators have finite moments, and under which their efficiency is comparable to that of importance sampling. Experiments illustrate unbiased estimators of the inverse of a normalizing constant, estimators of nested expectations, and combination of importance sampling with robust mean estimation methods.
item.dc:creator: George Deligiannidis (University of Oxford), Pierre E. Jacob (ESSEC Business School), El Mahdi Khribch (ESSEC Business School), Guanyang Wang (Rutgers University)

item.title: Perfect Clustering in Extremely Sparse Multilayer Networks with Groupwise Subspace Structure
item.description: arXiv:2507.19423v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The paper studies a multilayer network on the same collection of nodes, where each layer follows the Generalized Random Dot Product Graph Model. Furthermore, all layers can be partitioned into groups, each group with its own unique latent subspace structure, but otherwise the matrices of connection probabilities can all be different. This setting is extremely general and includes most multilayer network models as special cases. In addition, we are interested in the situation where the layer networks may be extremely sparse and, therefore, the layer-by-layer analysis is unreliable. This problem can also be seen as a generalization of the classic setting in which one recovers a shared structure across an entire collection of matrices, extending it to the case where such structures are shared only within specific groups of matrices. The key task in this setting is to recover the groups of layers with unique subspace structures, since, after that, the information in those groups of layers can be pooled together by well-studied methods. Until now, clustering of layers in such networks was based on layer-by-layer analysis, which required the multilayer network to be sufficiently dense. Our paper is the first to provide a tensor-based approach to the problem that combines information from all layers in an unconventional manner. Our theoretical results, established under intuitive and non-restrictive assumptions, assert that the new technique achieves perfect clustering under sparsity conditions that, up to logarithmic factors, coincide with the computational lower bound derived for a much simpler model. The paper also delivers a nuanced message about the applicability of the new technique.
item.dc:creator: Marianna Pensky

item.title: A Markov duration model with power-law decay via level-slope matching
item.description: arXiv:2607.20838v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a two-dimensional Markov duration model with power-law rate decay and a flexible residual distribution. The two state variables specify the excitation level and decay scale of a single power-law rate curve, and each update matches the level and slope jumps of a power-law Hawkes intensity. Under a sufficient stability condition, a finite residual mean, and a positive continuous residual density, the state at event times is positive Harris recurrent and converges geometrically in total variation to a unique invariant distribution. With unit exponential residuals, the sufficient region contains every parameter value for which the matched Hawkes process is subcritical. We apply the model to E-mini S\&P 500 futures and NVDA midquote durations at several price-change thresholds. Flexible residual laws improve likelihood-based fit, and power-law decay lowers one-step negative log predictive scores relative to exponential decay. An autoregressive conditional duration model generally leaves less residual autocorrelation, while forecast rankings vary with the price threshold and evaluation criterion.
